content: Urinary incontinence in women represents a significant health and economic challenge for society. Periurethral or transurethral injection of bulking agents is a minimally invasive surgical option for managing stress urinary incontinence (SUI) in adult women. This therapy involves injecting materials around or into the urethra to improve continence by increasing urethral resistance. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of periurethral or transurethral injection therapy in curing or improving urinary incontinence in women. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials where at least one treatment arm involved injection therapy. Fourteen trials involving 2004 women met the inclusion criteria, although one trial was excluded due to withdrawal from publication. The data from these trials were not suitable for meta-analysis because each trial was conducted independently, and the sample sizes were generally small with moderate methodological quality. One trial involving 45 women compared injection therapy with conservative treatment and demonstrated early benefits of injection therapy in terms of continence grade (risk ratio [RR] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.52 to 0.94) and quality of life (mean difference [MD] 0.54, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.92). However, another trial comparing autologous fat injection with placebo was terminated early due to safety concerns. Two trials compared injection therapy with surgical management. Both trials showed significantly better objective cure rates in the surgical group (RR 4.77, 95% CI 1.96 to 11.64; and RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.79). However, in one of these trials, the results did not reach statistical significance when analyzed using an intention-to-treat approach. Eight trials compared different bulking agents, including silicone particles, calcium hydroxylapatite, ethylene vinyl alcohol, carbon spheres, and dextranomer hyaluronic acid. None of these agents demonstrated clear superiority over collagen, and the results had wide confidence intervals. Notably, dextranomer hyaluronic acid was associated with significantly higher rates of injection site complications (16% versus 0% with collagen; RR 37.78, 95% CI 2.34 to 610.12). This product has since been withdrawn from the market. A comparison of periurethral and transurethral injection methods revealed similar outcomes, although the periurethral group had a higher rate of early complications, which was not statistically significant. One small trial of 30 women suggested a weak advantage in patient satisfaction for mid-urethral injection compared to bladder neck injection, but there was no significant difference in continence outcomes. The evidence base remains insufficient to provide definitive guidance for clinical practice. Interestingly, one trial found that placebo saline injection resulted in symptomatic improvement similar to that of bulking agent injection, raising questions about the mechanism of action behind the observed benefits. A small trial comparing silicone particles with pelvic floor muscle training suggested short-term benefits at three months, but the durability of these effects is unknown. This treatment was also associated with high rates of postoperative urinary retention and dysuria. Surgical treatments generally provided greater symptomatic improvement compared to injection therapy, but these benefits must be weighed against the higher risks associated with surgery. No clear conclusions could be drawn regarding the superiority of specific bulking agents, although dextranomer hyaluronic acid was linked to more local side effects and is no longer available for this indication. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether mid-urethral or bladder neck injection is superior. The use of autologous fat as a bulking agent serves as a reminder that periurethral injections can occasionally result in serious adverse effects. A brief economic analysis identified three studies suggesting that urethral bulking agents may be more cost-effective than retropubic mid-urethral slings, transobturator slings, or traditional sling procedures when used as an initial treatment in women without urethral hypermobility or as a secondary treatment following surgical failure, provided the volume of injection is minimal. However, when compared to traditional sling procedures as an initial treatment, urethral bulking agents may not be cost-effective over a longer follow-up period (e.g., 15 months post-surgery).
